To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

repetitive transcranial stimulation of the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) increased dopamine release in the putamen (as measured by PET), and that this increase in striatal dopamine release was associated with increased cognitive flexibility (as measured by fMRI).

(i) repetitive TMS (rTMS) applied over the frontal cortex increases striatal dopamine release, (ii) rTMS applied over frontal cortex reduces the functional coupling between the frontal cortex and striatum, and (iii) rTMS reduces cognitive flexibility by reducing the functional coupling between frontal cortex and putamen.

repetitive TMS of the human frontal cortex can modulate cognitive flexibility via topographically specific effects on the striatum, and that this modulation is associated with changes in functional connectivity between the frontal cortex and the striatum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms of cognitive flexibility.
the role of the frontal cortex in controlling cognitive flexibility.
the functional and topographical specificity of fronto-striatally mediated cognitive control.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the frontal cortex is able to control cognitive flexibility through the striatum.
our data show a topographically specific functional interaction between the human frontal and the putamen, which is modulated by repetitive TMS over the frontal cortex.
the human frontal lobe controls cognitive flexibility by topographically regulating striatal function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the frontal cortex controls cognitive switching via frontostriatal pathways, and that this control involves topographically specific fronto-striatoputamen connectivity.
we have demonstrated that cognitive flexibility depends on topographic control of striatal activity by the frontal cortex.
the frontal cortex can regulate the striatum, and this can have consequences for cognition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cognitive functions are not only controlled by the striatum, but also by other cortical regions.
the human frontal and parietal cortex are not interchangeable in their ability to control striatal function and, thus, cognitive flexibility.
the frontal cortex can be used to modulate the striatum and, in turn, to control cognitive flexibility.
